title: Behind the Curtain: Power-Family Intelligence Layer
editorialBoundary: This layer measures documented authority, asset control, institutional access, network centrality, advisory influence, succession position and operational activity. It is not a guilt score and does not infer wrongdoing, secret coordination or total control from family membership, wealth, marriage, attendance or social contact.

lanes.title: Proven Control
lanes.text: Legal authority, voting rights, beneficial ownership, trustee powers, executive office and documented appointment rights.

lanes.title: Documented Access
lanes.text: Board overlap, formal advisory position, repeated institutional access, policy participation and verified professional representation.

lanes.title: Bounded Inference
lanes.text: Transparent analysis derived from multiple documented links. It remains an inference and cannot become a factual accusation.

claims.claim: A single family bloc commands the major monetary, security, regulatory, technological and capital systems of the world.
claims.support: Some dynasties possess explicit state authority or durable corporate voting control.
claims.against: The source datasets show fragmented legal mandates, independent institutions, professional management, regulators, counterparties and competing states.
claims.missing: Authenticated cross-institution instructions, enforceable control rights or a documented command chain spanning the systems claimed.
claims.conclusion: Not established by the current public record.

claims.claim: Powerful surnames are irrelevant because institutions are impersonal.
claims.support: Institutions constrain individuals and often survive changes of leadership.
claims.against: Succession law, voting pools, foundations, holding companies and appointments can preserve multigenerational access.
claims.missing: Family-by-family control-chain evidence and transaction-level decision records.
claims.conclusion: Contradicted where authority or control rights are legally embedded; otherwise case-specific.

claims.claim: Public faces are always less important than hidden operators.
claims.support: Trustees, investment officers, senior advisers and board representatives can exercise operational authority without mass visibility.
claims.against: Heads of government, ruling monarchs and formal chairs may possess direct authority that cannot be reduced to advisers.
claims.missing: Decision records identifying who initiated, approved, blocked or implemented specific actions.
claims.conclusion: Sometimes true, never safe as a universal assumption.

unresolvedQuestions: Who possesses the final voting authority in each family holding, trust or foundation structure?
Which trustees can appoint or remove directors, beneficiaries, protectors or investment managers?
Who appoints the family-office chief executive and investment leadership?
Which adviser appears repeatedly across major transactions, disputes and succession events?
Which foundation grants create repeated access to policy-making institutions?
Which private companies remain beneficially opaque despite public-facing ownership claims?
Who represents the family during negotiations with governments, regulators or sovereign investors?
Which publicly active successor is accumulating board, foundation or investment authority?
Which relationship is merely social, and which produces a measurable decision or transfer of control?
What evidence would lower the current proximity-to-power score rather than only raise it?
reviewTriggers: Claims of secret control over a government or world event
